title: Hidden transverse-flow topology in partially coherent structured light
abstract: Partial coherence is commonly viewed as a mechanism that reduces contrast or smooths intensity structure. Here we show that it can also encode hidden transverse-flow topology. Starting from the cross-spectral density, we formulate a generalized transverse flux, an effective velocity field, and the associated flux trajectories for quasi-monochromatic partially coherent paraxial beams. This construction converts two-point correlation phases into local transport information and reduces to the usual coherent energy-flow picture in the single-mode limit. Because the generalized flux is obtained through a local differential operation on the cross-spectral density, the proposed trajectories can, in principle, be reconstructed from measurements of the complex second-order coherence function, without requiring direct measurement of individual optical paths. Two analytical beam families expose this hidden topology. In twisted Gaussian Schell-model beams, a Gaussian intensity hides a distributed rotational flow with nonzero vorticity. In Laguerre-Christoffel-Darboux beams, sources with identical intensity profiles can have different flux topology, producing either spiral or purely radial trajectories. Thus, intensity and coherence magnitude do not exhaust the physical information contained in the cross-spectral density: partial coherence can reorganize the hidden topology of transverse optical transport.
summary: The paper shows that partial coherence allows for the encoding of hidden transverse energy flow topologies invisible when only measuring light intensity. By deriving a generalized flux from the cross-spectral density, authors define an effective velocity field that maps out these flow trajectories. This proves that full physical information requires analyzing the off-diagonal phase structure of the CSD, not just its magnitude.
main_problem: To demonstrate that partial coherence encodes hidden transverse-flow topology, which is invisible when analyzing only the intensity profile of structured light.
main_result: The generalized transverse flux derived from the cross-spectral density reveals flow structures (like vorticity or circulation) in beams—such as TGSM or LCD beams—that are entirely masked by identical intensity measurements.
method: Formulating a generalized transverse flux and an effective velocity field using local differential operations on the two-point correlation function (CSD).
model_or_system: Quasi-monochromatic, paraxial partially coherent beams, analyzed using their cross-spectral density $W(\mathbf{r}_1, \mathbf{r}_2, z)$. Specific examples include Twisted Gaussian Schell-model and Liquid Crystal Display (LCD) sources.
key_observables: Generalized transverse flux ($\mathbf{J}$), effective velocity field ($\mathbf{v}_\perp$), circulation ($\Gamma$), vorticity ($\Omega$), and flow trajectories (spiral vs. radial).
important_parameters: Partial coherence level, beam type (TGSM, LCD), propagation distance ($z$).
main_assumptions: The beams are quasi-monochromatic and paraxial; the analysis relies on reconstructing quantities from the complex second-order coherence function.
figures_summary: Figures conceptually illustrate that the CSD contains both diagonal intensity content and off-diagonal correlation-phase information, which is used to extract the generalized transverse flux defining the flow field.
paper_structure: The paper develops a theoretical framework starting from the CSD to define a generalized flux ($\mathbf{J}$), derives an effective velocity field ($\mathbf{v}_\perp = \mathbf{J}/I$), and then applies this formalism to specific beam families (TGSM, LCD) to contrast their hidden flow topologies against their measured intensities.
why_interesting: This work extends the understanding of optical coherence beyond simple intensity measurements by introducing a transport-based diagnostic derived from higher-order correlation functions, analogous to current density in quantum field theory.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Conceptual structure of the generalized flux-trajectory formulation. The cross-spectral density W(r1, r2, z) contains both the diagonal intensity content and the off-diagonal correlation-phase information. The former gives the spectral density I(r, z) = W(r, r, z), whereas the latter gives access to the generalized transverse flux J. Together, I and J define the effective velocity field v⊥= J/I. The topology of this velocity field is characterized through streamlines and diagnostics such as circulation Γ, vorticity Ω, and accumulated angular displacement Θ. The same intensity distribution can therefore support different transverse-flow topologies.

FIG. 2. Hidden rotational flow in TGSM beams. The background color represents the normalized Gaussian spectral density S(r, z), shown in coordinates scaled by the propagated beam size w(z). White curves are streamlines of the generalized transverse velocity field at z/Λ0 = 1. (a) In the untwisted case, µ0Λ0 = 0, so that µ(z)Λ0 = 0 for all z, the flow is purely radial. (b) For a twisted TGSM beam with µ0Λ0 = 1, at the displayed plane z/Λ0 = 1 one has µ(z)Λ0 = 1/2. The intensity remains Gaussian, but the nonseparable coherence phase produces an azimuthal component vφ = µ(z)r, leading to spiral streamlines. (c) Accumulated angular displacement ΘTGSM(z) = µ0Λ0 arctan (z/Λ0) for several values...

FIG. 3. Hidden transverse-flow topology in LCD beams. The background color represents the normalized intensity IN,m(r, z), which is the same in both cases. White curves show streamlines of the generalized transverse velocity field at z = zR. (a) A single-charge LCD source with topological charge +m displays spiral flow because vφ = m/(kr). (b) A balanced superposition of opposite charges +m and −m has the same intensity profile, but the azimuthal flux cancels and the flow is purely radial. (c) Radial intensity profile and circulation normalized to 2πm/k. The single-charge source has Γ+m = 2πm/k, whereas the balanced source has Γ±m = 0. Parameters: N = 3, m = 2, w0 = 1, zR = 1, k = 2, and...

FIG. 4. Schematic classification of hidden transverse-flow topology in the analytical cases considered in this work. A TGSM beam with twist displays distributed rotational transport, with vφ = µr, circulation Γ = 2πµr2, and uniform vorticity Ω= 2µ. A single-charge LCD beam displays angular transport of topological origin, with vφ = m/(kr) and radius-independent circulation Γ = 2πm/k, while the vorticity vanishes away from the singular core. A balanced LCD source with opposite charges +m and −m has the same radial intensity profile as the single-charge case, but the azimuthal flux cancels exactly, giving vφ = 0, Γ = 0, and Ω= 0.
